projects.name: Cloud-Backed Portfolio
projects.purpose: Build a portfolio that is also a hands-on DevOps system, demonstrating cloud architecture, Infrastructure as Code, automated validation, secure cloud authentication, protected releases, serverless APIs, persistence, testing, observability, and operational documentation.

architecture.frontend: React + TypeScript single-page application built with Vite. Source lives in Jeysibn/portfolio; the generated frontend/app/dist artifact is published to the dedicated Jeysibn/jeysibn.github.io repository and served at the root GitHub Pages domain.
architecture.backend: Python 3.11 Azure Functions using the Python v2 programming model.
architecture.database: Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL with PortfolioDB, Counter, and VisitorIPs containers.
architecture.infrastructure: Terraform with the AzureRM provider in Azure Korea Central.
architecture.terraform_state: Remote Terraform state stored in Azure Blob Storage.
architecture.observability: Workspace-based Azure Application Insights and Log Analytics provide request, latency, failure, exception, and structured operational telemetry.
architecture.ai: An OpenAI-compatible API integration powers a portfolio-specific AI assistant. The frontend intentionally uses model-neutral branding so backend model changes do not require a frontend branding change.
architecture.authentication: GitHub Actions authenticates to Azure using GitHub OIDC federation with Microsoft Entra ID instead of a reusable Azure client secret.
architecture.branching: Two-branch model: dev for development/integration and main for protected production.

azure_resources: Standard LRS Storage Account for Azure Functions
Azure Cosmos DB account using the NoSQL API and free-tier configuration
Log Analytics workspace with cost guardrails

cicd.development: Pushes to dev validate the React frontend with dependency installation, strict TypeScript typechecking, a Vite production build and artifact verification, plus Python dependency/syntax/Ruff/pytest checks and Terraform formatting/init-without-backend/validation.
cicd.pull_request: A dev-to-main PR performs production-readiness validation including frontend artifact creation, backend dependency auditing, tests, Azure Function package creation, Azure OIDC authentication, remote-backend Terraform planning, and a final Production Ready gate.
cicd.production: Merges to main trigger path-specific workflows. Frontend changes build frontend/app/dist in Jeysibn/portfolio, then publish that artifact to the dedicated Jeysibn/jeysibn.github.io repository and verify https://jeysibn.github.io/. Backend changes deploy to Azure Functions and run API smoke checks; Terraform changes run a production plan and apply.
cicd.concurrency: CI cancels obsolete development/PR runs while production Terraform deployment does not cancel in-progress applies.

security_and_reliability: Uses short-lived GitHub OIDC tokens for Azure authentication instead of storing an Azure service principal client secret.
Uses a dedicated GitHub Actions Pages publishing token only for cross-repository publication to Jeysibn/jeysibn.github.io; it is separate from Azure OIDC authentication.
Hashes visitor IP addresses with SHA-256 before storage.
Visitor/rate-limit records use a Cosmos DB TTL of 86400 seconds.
Backend dependencies are audited during PR validation.
Application and infrastructure changes are tested before production merge.
The AI client is lazily initialized so a missing AI API key cannot prevent Azure Functions from indexing unrelated routes.
The AI provider API key is stored as a GitHub Actions secret and passed to Terraform as a sensitive variable to configure the Azure Function App environment.
features: Unique visitor counter backed by Cosmos DB.
Per-IP AI chat rate limit of 10 messages per hour.
Live Azure Functions health monitor with build-derived release metadata and Manila time.
Interactive whole-card project details with lightweight WebP architecture previews and full-resolution diagrams loaded only on explicit zoom.
Automated frontend, backend, and infrastructure deployment with post-deployment verification.
testing: pytest tests cover visitor-counter logic, AI chat behavior, route behavior, and lazy AI client initialization.
Tests use mocks/stubs and do not call real Azure Cosmos DB or the external AI provider.
operational_lessons: A deployment pipeline can report successful package deployment even when runtime routes are not healthy, so deployment success and runtime readiness should be treated as separate signals.
Optional external integrations should not be initialized at module import time because configuration failures can break function discovery.
Post-deployment health/API checks and Azure-native observability are implemented so runtime verification follows deployment rather than relying on upload success alone.
cost_awareness: Uses Azure Functions Linux Consumption (Y1), Standard LRS storage, and Cosmos DB free tier to stay suitable for an Azure for Students subscription.
Log Analytics uses bounded retention and an ingestion cap as telemetry cost guardrails.
Jerome uses an Azure for Students subscription for this project.

projects.name: Enterprise GitOps Homelab
projects.experience_context: Personal home-lab project designed to apply production-style infrastructure and operational practices.
projects.purpose: Build a fully automated, self-healing, observable local Kubernetes environment using Infrastructure as Code and GitOps, with the Git repository acting as the source of truth.

current_physical_environment.location: The homelab hardware is located at Jerome's parents' house.
current_physical_environment.proxmox_host: One refurbished/repurposed laptop runs Proxmox VE.
current_physical_environment.kubernetes_scale: The current K3s environment runs one Kubernetes master/server node.
current_physical_environment.remote_access_device: A Raspberry Pi 4B provides remote network access to the homelab using Tailscale VPN; it is not currently a Kubernetes node.
current_physical_environment.runtime_observation: The Proxmox host has been running for roughly one month, and Jerome has not experienced hardware errors or observed downtime during that period.
current_physical_environment.uptime_guardrail: Treat the roughly one-month observation as personal observation, not a formal availability SLA or independently measured uptime percentage.

architecture.virtualization: Proxmox virtual machines provisioned with Terraform.
architecture.cluster: K3s lightweight Kubernetes. The current environment is a single-node K3s server/master deployment.
architecture.gitops: Argo CD using the App-of-Apps pattern and sync waves.
architecture.networking: Calico CNI, MetalLB LoadBalancer IP address management, Traefik ingress, and Cert-Manager for TLS.
architecture.storage: Longhorn CSI storage is part of the repository architecture; claims of high availability should be qualified because the current Kubernetes environment is single-node.
architecture.observability: Prometheus for metrics, Loki for logs, and Grafana for visualization.
architecture.remote_access: Tailscale provides remote connectivity through a Raspberry Pi 4B.

gitops_workflow: Develop Terraform or Kubernetes YAML changes in Git.
GitHub Actions validates infrastructure/manifests using tools such as kubeconform and tflint.
Approved changes are merged to main.
Argo CD detects drift and reconciles the K3s cluster to the repository state.
engineering_practices: Infrastructure as Code for VM provisioning.
Sync waves for ordered application deployment.
CI quality gates for Helm/Kubernetes validation and security misconfiguration checks.
Separation between raw Kubernetes manifests and Helm value overrides.
Automated TLS, local DNS, storage, and observability services.

earlier_cluster_experiment.topology: Jerome's first homelab testing used an old laptop running Ubuntu Server together with a Raspberry Pi as two K3s nodes.
earlier_cluster_experiment.challenge: The biggest challenge was operating a cluster across different CPU architectures on the two hardware platforms.
earlier_cluster_experiment.lesson: The mixed-architecture setup exposed compatibility and deployment considerations that do not appear when all cluster nodes use the same architecture.

projects.disaster_recovery: The repository documents a bootstrap process intended to rebuild the cluster from bare metal in under 15 minutes by provisioning VMs, installing K3s/CNI, installing Argo CD, and applying the root App-of-Apps manifest. Do not state that Jerome has personally benchmarked a sub-15-minute rebuild unless the knowledge base is later updated with a measured test result.
problems_addressed: Invalid Kubernetes manifests and configuration errors
Remote administration of a homelab located at another residence
Mixed CPU architecture compatibility during early K3s experimentation
